group.passage:
For much of the twentieth century, Costa Rica’s forests were seen mainly as land waiting to be cleared. From 1950 on, the country tied its growth to farm exports, and large areas of forest were turned into fields and, above all, into pasture for cattle. During the 1970s and 1980s, Costa Rica was losing its forests faster than almost any other country in the world.
Two changes helped turn things around. First, economic reforms in the 1980s made raising crops and cattle on poor forest land far less profitable, and as meat prices fell, many pastures were simply abandoned. Young forests began to grow back on them. Second, a forest law passed in 1996 recognized that forests do more than supply wood: they store carbon, protect sources of water, shelter wildlife, and offer scenery that attracts visitors. On this basis, the government began paying landowners to keep existing forest, plant new trees, or grow trees alongside their crops. Most of the money came from a tax on fuel, and by 2005 about 250,000 hectares were under contract, nearly all of it existing forest that would be left standing.
The chart compares Costa Rica with three other Central American countries from 1990 onward. The World Bank now describes Costa Rica as the first tropical country to reverse the loss of its forests, which today cover close to 60 percent of its land. The effort has also brought international rewards. In 2019, the country received the United Nations’ Champion of the Earth award, and in 2022 it became the first country in Latin America to be paid by a World Bank fund for cutting the carbon released from its forests.
The success, however, rests on a few fragile supports. Much of the regained cover is young forest or tree plantations, which are worth less to nature than the old forests that were lost. The payment program, for its part, has depended heavily on the fuel tax and on short-term help from foreign donors. Keeping forests standing, it seems, takes steady money as well as good laws.

translation_zh.text:
在二十世紀的大部分時間裡，哥斯大黎加的森林大多被看成等著被砍伐的土地。從 1950 年起，這個國家把經濟成長寄託在農產品出口上，大片森林被改成農田，而且主要是改成養牛的牧場。在 1970 和 1980 年代，哥斯大黎加失去森林的速度幾乎比世界上任何國家都快。
有兩項轉變幫助扭轉了局面。第一，1980 年代的經濟改革讓在貧瘠林地上種作物、養牛變得很不划算；隨著肉價下跌，許多牧場就這樣被放棄了，新生的森林開始在那裡長回來。第二，1996 年通過的一部森林法承認，森林不只能提供木材：它們能儲存碳、保護水源、庇護野生動物，還能提供吸引遊客的景觀。政府據此開始付錢給地主，請他們保留現有的森林、種植新樹，或在作物旁種樹。經費大多來自燃料稅；到了 2005 年，約有 25 萬公頃的土地簽了合約，其中幾乎全是會被保留下來的原有森林。
圖表比較了 1990 年以來哥斯大黎加和另外三個中美洲國家。世界銀行現在形容哥斯大黎加是第一個扭轉森林流失的熱帶國家，如今森林覆蓋了它將近 60% 的土地。這些努力也帶來了國際肯定：2019 年，哥斯大黎加獲得聯合國的「地球衛士獎」；2022 年，它成為第一個因減少森林碳排放而獲得世界銀行基金付款的拉丁美洲國家。
然而，這份成功建立在幾個脆弱的支柱上。重新長回來的森林有很大一部分是新生林或人工林，它們對大自然的價值比不上已經失去的老森林。付費計畫則一直高度依賴燃料稅，以及外國捐助者的短期援助。看來，要讓森林繼續屹立，既需要好的法律，也需要穩定的經費。
【圖】四個中美洲國家的森林面積占國土面積比例（1990–2020，%）：哥斯大黎加、尼加拉瓜、宏都拉斯、瓜地馬拉。

reference_answers: Costa Rica could charge water companies a small fee, because forests protect the sources of water that these companies use.
The country could add a small fee for visitors to forest areas, since the scenery that attracts them is one of the services that forests provide.

B.explanation_zh: 答非所問：付費計畫的經費和燃料稅、外援連在一起，不是和遊客連在一起；遊客能不能來不是付費計畫本身的問題。

D.evidence: Young forests began to grow back on them.
D.explanation_zh: 新生林是在被放棄的牧場上自然長回來的，文中沒有說它的生長速度和燃料用量有關。

problems: 第一段首句「For much of the twentieth century, Costa Rica’s forests were seen mainly as land waiting to be cleared」：事實單沒有這一條（f1 只寫 1950 年起森林變成牧場與農田）。World Bank OED（s3）寫農民為了取得土地所有權盡量砍伐森林、發展觀念與農產品出口綁在一起，說法有來源支持，但 much of the twentieth century 的時間範圍比事實單寬。不影響任何小題，列 warn 供人工審核，建議補進事實單
details.method_zh: 逐句比對選文、圖表（caption、description、chart 數值）、題幹與選項中的事實與數字和事實單；圖表數值重新下載來源資料比對；可開啟的來源逐條確認（見各條 note）。
